html:
Dënësųłinë́ Nëné is the land of the Dënësųłinë́, or Chipewyan, a Dene people of the northern forest and the edge of the tundra, from Great Slave Lake and Lake Athabasca east toward Hudson Bay. Their language is one of the Athabaskan languages. Denendeh, the land of the people, is the Dene name for the whole Dene north.

They followed the barren ground caribou, which moved between the tundra in summer and the forest in winter, and fished the many lakes.

The Hudson's Bay Company opened trade with them through its posts on Hudson Bay. In 1715 a Dënësųłinë́ woman, Thanadelthur, helped make peace between her people and the Cree so trade could flow. The chief Matonabbee guided Samuel Hearne overland to the Arctic coast in 1770 to 1772. A smallpox epidemic in 1781 and 1782 killed a large share of the people.

They signed Treaty 8 and Treaty 10 in the early 1900s. Today Dënësųłinë́ communities lie in Saskatchewan, Alberta, Manitoba, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut. Neighbours: Yellowknives and Inuit.
